noteBlocks.md: Crude oil is a **mixture** of many **hydrocarbons**, compounds of hydrogen and carbon only, and most of them are **alkanes**, $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$. Three facts about it carry marks: it is a **finite resource**; it is the **main source of hydrocarbons**; and it is a **feedstock for the petrochemical industry**, the raw material for plastics, medicines and detergents.
**Finite** means it will run out. Crude oil formed over millions of years from the remains of tiny sea creatures buried under mud and rock, and it is being used far faster than any new oil forms.

noteBlocks.stem: Explain why crude oil is described as a finite resource, but wood from a managed forest is not. [2]

steps.working: Crude oil took millions of years to form and is being used far faster than any new oil can form, so one day it will run out: it is finite.
steps.decision: Finite means it will run out; give the reason as well as the word.

steps.working: Wood from a managed forest is replaced as it is used: new trees are planted and grow back within a lifetime, so it is renewable.
steps.decision: The near-miss: wood is burned as a fuel too, but it is replaced, and that is the test crude oil fails.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is a finite resource?
noteBlocks.explain: Coal, like crude oil, took millions of years to form and will run out, as step 1 of See it said of crude oil. Wood and sugar cane grow back, so they are renewable.

optionNotes.why: New trees are planted and grow back within a lifetime, so this fuel is replaced as it is used.
Sugar cane is grown again every year, so the ethanol made from it can be replaced.

twin.explain: Sugar cane grows again each year, so ethanol made from it is replaced as it is used, like the wood in step 2 of See it. Natural gas and crude oil will run out.

optionNotes.why: Natural gas formed with crude oil over millions of years and is being used up far faster than it forms.
Crude oil took millions of years to form and will run out: it is the finite one.

noteBlocks.text: 2. Fractional distillation: the points that score

noteBlocks.md: The crude oil is **heated** until it **evaporates**. The vapour rises up a column that is **hottest at the bottom** and **coolest at the top**, so it cools as it climbs. Each hydrocarbon **condenses** back to a liquid at the level where **the temperature matches its boiling point**, and is drawn off there. The process is **continuous**: crude oil goes in and the fractions come out all the time.

noteBlocks.title: Why chain length decides the level
noteBlocks.md: Longer chains attract each other more strongly, so they have higher boiling points. A long-chain vapour condenses as soon as it rises into a slightly cooler part, near the bottom; a short chain stays a gas almost to the top. A **fraction** is a group of hydrocarbons with boiling points close together.

noteBlocks.stem: A hydrocarbon in crude oil boils at 200 °C. Use the column with temperatures shown to describe how fractional distillation separates it, and name the fraction it ends up in. [4]

steps.working: The crude oil is heated to about 400 °C at the bottom, far above 200 °C, so the hydrocarbon evaporates.
steps.decision: Evaporates is the scheme's word for the first change; heating alone earns nothing.

steps.working: Its vapour rises up the column and cools, because the column gets cooler the higher it goes.
steps.decision: Rising and cooling is what lets the hydrocarbons part company.

steps.working: At the level where the temperature has fallen to 200 °C, its boiling point, it condenses back to a liquid.
steps.decision: Two marks in one line: condenses, and the temperature matching the boiling point.

steps.working: It is drawn off at that outlet, so it ends up in the kerosene fraction.
steps.decision: Read the fraction off the outlet whose temperature matches the boiling point.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Fractional Distillation of Crude Oil"
noteBlocks.why: A second view of the column and its fractions, beside our own worked steps.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the column with temperatures shown, a hydrocarbon boils at 70 °C. In which fraction is it collected?
noteBlocks.explain: It condenses where the temperature has fallen to 70 °C, and that outlet is petrol, just as step 3 of See it found the 200 °C level for kerosene.

optionNotes.why: Naphtha's outlet is at 120 °C; a vapour that boils at 70 °C is still a gas there and rises higher.
The refinery gases leave at 30 °C; a hydrocarbon that boils at 70 °C has condensed lower down.

twin.prompt: On the same column, a hydrocarbon boils at 330 °C. In which fraction is it collected?
twin.explain: It meets its boiling point, 330 °C, at the fuel oils outlet and condenses there: step 3 of See it, lower down the column.

optionNotes.why: Diesel's outlet is at 270 °C, cooler than 330 °C; this hydrocarbon has condensed below that level.
Bitumen stays at the 400 °C bottom; a vapour that boils at 330 °C rises above it before it condenses.

noteBlocks.text: 3. The seven fractions and their uses

noteBlocks.md: Learn the order and the uses together, because a question can give either one. Kerosene and naphtha are the pair to learn with most care: kerosene flies (aircraft), naphtha makes things (chemicals and plastics). Bitumen is also called tar.

noteBlocks.stem: One fraction leaves the column between petrol and kerosene. Name it and give its use. [2]

steps.working: Counting down from the top: refinery gases, petrol, then naphtha, then kerosene. So the fraction between petrol and kerosene is naphtha.
steps.decision: Write the order out before you answer: the position decides the fraction.

steps.working: Naphtha is used to make chemicals and plastics.
steps.decision: Give the use in the specification's sense: it is the chemical industry's raw material, not a fuel.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which crude-oil fraction is used as a fuel for ships?
noteBlocks.explain: Fuel oils fuel ships. As in step 1 of See it, use the order: fuel oils sit below diesel and just above bitumen.

optionNotes.why: Diesel fuels cars and trains; the heavier fuel oils, just below it, fuel ships.
Bitumen is far too thick to burn in an engine; it surfaces roads and roofs.

twin.prompt: What are refinery gases used for?
twin.explain: Refinery gases, first in the order of step 1 of See it, are sold as bottled gas for cooking and heating.

optionNotes.why: Aircraft run on kerosene, a liquid fraction from much lower down the column.
That is bitumen, the fraction at the very bottom, not the gases at the top.

noteBlocks.md: The column gives more long-chain fractions than anyone wants and less petrol than drivers need. **Cracking** fixes the mismatch: it **breaks long saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) into shorter molecules that are worth more**, and **some of the products are unsaturated (alkenes)**. The shorter alkanes are used as fuels; the alkenes are the raw material for plastics.

Cracking is a chemical reaction, because new substances form. Fractional distillation only separates substances that were already there, and polymerisation does the opposite of cracking: it joins small alkene molecules into long chains.

noteBlocks.stem: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₉H₂₀ + C₃H₆. Explain why the reaction above counts as cracking. [4]

steps.working: C₁₂H₂₆ is a large saturated hydrocarbon: an alkane, CnH2n+2, with single bonds only.
steps.decision: Start with the reactant: the scheme wants it named as a large saturated hydrocarbon.

steps.working: It is broken down into smaller molecules: chains of 9 and 3 carbons.
steps.decision: Broken down into smaller ones is the heart of the definition.

steps.working: The smaller alkane, C₉H₂₀, is in the petrol range, so it is more useful than the long chain it came from.
steps.decision: More useful, or in greater demand, is the point most often left out.

steps.working: C₃H₆ fits CnH2n: it is unsaturated, an alkene.
steps.decision: Name the alkene and say it is unsaturated: that is the fourth mark.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Cracking"
noteBlocks.why: Cracking explained a second way, beside our own worked steps.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these changes is cracking?
options: a long alkane broken into a shorter alkane and an alkene
small alkene molecules joined into one long chain
crude oil separated into fractions by boiling point
noteBlocks.answer: a long alkane broken into a shorter alkane and an alkene
noteBlocks.explain: Cracking breaks a long molecule into smaller ones, some of them unsaturated, as steps 2 and 4 of See it showed. Joining alkenes is polymerisation; separating by boiling point is fractional distillation.

optionNotes.option: small alkene molecules joined into one long chain
optionNotes.why: That is the opposite change: joining alkenes into a long chain is polymerisation.

optionNotes.option: crude oil separated into fractions by boiling point
optionNotes.why: That only separates what was already there; cracking makes new, smaller molecules.

twin.prompt: Which of these is NOT a reason for cracking?
options: to separate crude oil into its fractions
to make more petrol than the column supplies
twin.answer: to separate crude oil into its fractions
twin.explain: Separating is the column's job. Cracking makes more petrol and makes alkenes, the two products steps 3 and 4 of See it named.

optionNotes.option: to make more petrol than the column supplies
optionNotes.why: That is a real reason: the shorter alkanes from cracking are petrol, which is in greater demand.
That is a real reason: the alkenes that cracking makes are the raw material for plastics.

noteBlocks.md: No atoms are made or lost in cracking, so the products' carbons add up to the reactant's, and so do their hydrogens. To find a missing product, **subtract**: carbons from carbons, hydrogens from hydrogens. Then check it: an alkane product fits $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$ and an alkene product fits $\ce{C_nH_{2n}}$.

noteBlocks.stem: C₁₄H₃₀ is cracked into C₃H₆ and one other product. Find the formula of the other product. [1]

steps.working: Carbons: 14 − 3 = 11.
steps.decision: Subtract the alkene's carbons from the reactant's.

steps.working: Hydrogens: 30 − 6 = 24, so the other product is C₁₁H₂₄.
steps.decision: Then the hydrogens, the same way.

steps.working: Check: 2 × 11 + 2 = 24, so C₁₁H₂₄ is an alkane and the equation balances.
steps.decision: A check with the general formula catches a slip before the examiner does.

noteBlocks.prompt: C₁₃H₂₈ is cracked into C₄H₈ and one other product. How many carbon atoms does the other product have?
noteBlocks.explain: 13 − 4 = 9: subtract the alkene's carbons, as step 1 of See it did. The other product is C₉H₂₀.

twin.prompt: C₁₈H₃₈ is cracked into C₆H₁₂ and one other product. How many hydrogen atoms does the other product have?
twin.explain: 38 − 12 = 26: subtract the hydrogens, as step 2 of See it did. The other product is C₁₂H₂₆.

noteBlocks.md:
**Word-select.** You may be given evaporate, condense and boiling beside melt, freeze and melting. The column needs evaporate, condense and boiling: nothing melts or freezes in it (2024).
**Why it is cracking [4].** Four points: a large saturated hydrocarbon; broken into smaller molecules; more useful; some unsaturated (alkenes). Name the molecules in the equation (2021).

**What finite means [1].** It will run out: it cannot be replaced once it is used (2026).
**Kerosene or naphtha.** Kerosene fuels aircraft; naphtha makes chemicals and plastics. Bitumen, also called tar, surfaces roads and roofs (2024; 2019).

noteBlocks.title: Where these marks went
noteBlocks.md: In 2024 few candidates described fractional distillation well, even at Foundation with a word list to choose from, and the uses of kerosene and naphtha were less well known than the use of bitumen. For the name of the process, thermal and catalytic cracking were both accepted.

noteBlocks.stem: A student writes: 'The crude oil is warmed until it melts. The liquid climbs the column and freezes at the level that matches its melting point.' Mark it out of 3 and correct it.

steps.working: 'Melts' is the wrong change: crude oil is already a liquid, and heating turns it into a vapour.
steps.decision: The first mark wants the change from a liquid to a gas.

steps.working: 'Freezes' is the wrong change too: as the vapour cools it turns back into a liquid.
steps.decision: The second mark wants the change from a gas back to a liquid.

steps.working: 'Melting point' is the wrong temperature: a vapour turns back to a liquid at its boiling point. As written: 0 out of 3.
steps.decision: The third mark wants the temperature matched to the boiling point.

noteBlocks.prompt: A word-select offers evaporate, melt and freeze. Which word fits 'Heating the crude oil makes the hydrocarbons …'?
noteBlocks.explain: Heating turns the liquid into a vapour, the change step 1 of See it named: evaporate. Melting turns a solid into a liquid, and crude oil is a liquid already.

optionNotes.why: Melting turns a solid into a liquid, but crude oil is a liquid already; heating turns it into a vapour.
Freezing needs cooling, not heating, and it turns a liquid into a solid.

twin.prompt: Which word fits 'As the vapour cools higher up the column, it … back to a liquid'?
twin.explain: Cooling turns the vapour back into a liquid, the change in step 2 of See it: it condenses. Freezing would turn a liquid into a solid.

optionNotes.why: Freezing turns a liquid into a solid; here a vapour is turning back into a liquid.
Evaporating is the change on the way up, from liquid to vapour; cooling reverses it.

noteBlocks.prompt: An answer to 'Explain why this is cracking [4]' reads: 'A large saturated alkane is broken down into smaller, more useful molecules.' Which point is missing?
options: some of the products are unsaturated (alkenes)
the products are heavier than the reactant
noteBlocks.answer: some of the products are unsaturated (alkenes)
noteBlocks.explain: The fourth point is the unsaturated product, the alkene that step 4 of See it in section 4 named. Heat and heavier products are not part of the definition.

optionNotes.why: Energy is not one of the four points; the missing one is about the kind of molecule made.

optionNotes.option: the products are heavier than the reactant
optionNotes.why: The products are smaller than the reactant: breaking it down is the whole point.

twin.prompt: Another answer reads: 'A large alkane is broken into smaller molecules, some of them alkenes.' Which point is missing?
options: the smaller molecules are more useful
twin.answer: the smaller molecules are more useful
twin.explain: More useful, or in greater demand, is the point left out: the one step 3 of See it in section 4 made about the petrol-range alkane.

optionNotes.why: Reacting with oxygen is combustion; cracking breaks the molecule without burning it.
Alkenes are unsaturated: they have a double bond, and the answer already names them.

items.stem: What happens to a liquid when it reaches its boiling point?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 — changes of state; you are not expected to have met fractional distillation yet

options.feedback: It boils and becomes a vapour. Running that backwards — vapour to liquid — is condensing, and the column depends on both.
That is freezing, which happens at the melting point instead. Boiling makes a gas.
The temperature holds steady while it boils, but the liquid is busily turning into gas.

items.stem: In the alkanes, what happens to the boiling point as the chain gets longer?

options.feedback: Longer chains attract each other more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them. The whole column is built on that.
The opposite: methane boils at −162 °C and butane at −1 °C. The trend rises.
If it stayed the same nothing would separate in the tower at all.

items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 — mixtures and compounds

options.text: two or more substances that are not chemically joined
options.feedback: Not joined, so they can be separated by physical means — which is exactly what the tower does.

options.text: two or more elements chemically bonded together
options.feedback: That is a compound. Crude oil is a mixture of compounds, which is why distillation can separate it.

options.text: a substance made of one kind of atom
options.feedback: That is an element. Crude oil is nothing like that simple.

options.text: a finite mixture of hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes
options.feedback: A mixture, finite, and mostly alkanes: all three are marking points in different questions.

options.text: a single compound with one formula
options.feedback: If it were one compound it would boil at one temperature and the column would be pointless.
Two errors: it is finite, not renewable, and its hydrocarbons are mostly saturated alkanes.
Hydrocarbons are compounds of two elements, not elements themselves.

items.stem: In a fractionating column, where is it hottest?

options.feedback: Hot at the bottom, cool at the top. Everything else about the tower follows from that.
The other way round. If the top were hottest, nothing would ever condense on the way up.

options.text: it is the same temperature all the way up
options.feedback: Then every fraction would condense in the same place and nothing would be separated.
The heat comes in at the bottom with the vaporised oil, so that is the hottest point.

items.stem: Which fraction is used as a fuel for aircraft?
items.skill: Match a fraction to its use

options.feedback: Kerosene. Keep it paired with naphtha in your head, because those two are the ones that get swapped.
Naphtha goes to the chemical works to make plastics and other chemicals, not into an aeroplane.
Bitumen is the thick residue used to surface roads and roofs.
Refinery gases are bottled for cooking and heating.

items.stem: Why does a fraction with a long chain leave the column low down?

options.text: it has a high boiling point, so it condenses while the vapour is still hot
options.feedback: Boiling point is the link between chain length and height in the tower.

options.text: it is heavier, so gravity pulls it down
options.feedback: Weight is not what sorts them: the vapours all rise. It is the temperature at which each one condenses.
Fractional distillation is a physical separation; no reaction happens in the tower.

options.text: it has a low boiling point
options.feedback: A low boiling point would keep it a gas for longer and carry it to the top. Long chains boil high.

options.text: breaks long alkanes apart into shorter molecules, some of them alkenes
options.feedback: Long to short, and some of what comes out is unsaturated. Both halves are marked.

options.text: joins small molecules into larger ones
options.feedback: That is polymerisation, which comes later. Cracking goes the other way.

options.text: separates crude oil into its fractions
options.feedback: That is fractional distillation, a physical process. Cracking is a chemical reaction that breaks bonds.

options.text: burns the heavy fractions to make heat
options.feedback: That is combustion. Cracking keeps the atoms and rearranges them into more useful molecules.

indicativeContent.point: The crude oil is heated so that the hydrocarbons evaporate.
The vapours rise up the column.
The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top.
Each fraction condenses where the temperature matches its boiling point.
Long chains have high boiling points and are collected low down.
Short chains have low boiling points and are collected near the top.
Two fractions named with a correct use, for example kerosene as a fuel for aircraft and bitumen for surfacing roads.

scheme.for: a banded description of the separation and the reason behind it: heating and evaporation, the vapours rising, the temperature gradient, condensing at the matching boiling point, long chains low and short chains high, and two named fractions with their uses
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Three steps, then the reason, then two named fractions.
The reason is about boiling points, not about weight.
parts.workedSolution: The crude oil is heated until the hydrocarbons evaporate, and the vapours rise up the column. The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top, so as a vapour rises it cools. Each fraction condenses at the height where the temperature has fallen to its boiling point, and is drawn off there. Long chains attract each other strongly and have high boiling points, so they condense low down; short chains have low boiling points and stay as vapour until near the top. Kerosene, collected part-way up, is used as a fuel for aircraft, and bitumen, left at the bottom, is used to surface roads and roofs.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niall is asked: 'Describe how crude oil is separated by fractional distillation, and say why bitumen is collected at the bottom. [4]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The crude oil is heated and the hydrocarbons evaporate.
The vapours rise up the column, which is hottest at the bottom.
Each fraction condenses where the temperature matches its boiling point.
Bitumen is collected at the bottom because it is the heaviest and gravity pulls it down.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The first three lines are a full-mark description. The last line swaps the mechanism: every fraction rises as a vapour, and what differs is the temperature at which each one condenses. Bitumen's chains are long, so its boiling point is high and it condenses almost at once, near the hot bottom.
correction: Bitumen is collected at the bottom because its long chains give it a very high boiling point, so it condenses as soon as the vapour cools.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four marks: the description is complete and correct. The one that goes is the explanation, because gravity is not what sorts the tower — boiling point is. Whenever you explain a height in the column, say boiling point.

findTheMistake.stem:
Orla is asked: 'Give the use of each of these fractions: petrol, kerosene and bitumen. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Petrol is a fuel for cars.
Kerosene is used to make chemicals and plastics.
Bitumen is used to surface roads and roofs.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 gives kerosene the use of naphtha. Kerosene is the fuel for aircraft; naphtha is the fraction the chemical industry turns into chemicals and plastics. The other two lines are right.
correction: Kerosene is a fuel for aircraft.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: petrol and bitumen stand. Keep the pair apart with one phrase each: kerosene flies, naphtha makes things.

prompts.prompt: Give three things the specification says about crude oil.
prompts.answer: It is a finite resource, it is the main source of hydrocarbons, and it is the feedstock of the petrochemical industry.

prompts.prompt: What are the fractions from crude oil mostly made of, and what is their general formula?
prompts.answer: Alkanes, with the general formula CnH2n+2.

prompts.prompt: Name the seven fractions in order from the top of the column.
prompts.answer: refinery gases, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oils, bitumen.

prompts.prompt: Kerosene and naphtha are the two fractions most often confused. What is each one used for?
prompts.answer: Kerosene is a fuel for aircraft; naphtha is used for making chemicals and plastics.

Which crude-oil fraction is used as a fuel for aircraft?
What does cracking break long alkanes into?
prompts.answer: Shorter, more useful molecules, some of them alkenes.

findings.asked: Name compounds of hydrogen and carbon only, complete a word-select on fractional distillation, and match four fractions to their uses.
findings.wentWrong: Even with the word list, the processes of fractional distillation were unfamiliar. Bitumen's use was well known, but the uses of kerosene and naphtha were not.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Chose evaporate, condense and boiling, and kept kerosene (aircraft) apart from naphtha (chemicals and plastics).
findings.rule: Evaporate on the way up, condense where the temperature matches the boiling point; kerosene flies, naphtha makes things.

findings.asked: Define a hydrocarbon, describe fractional distillation in three points, and name the process that breaks large saturated hydrocarbons into smaller ones.
findings.wentWrong: Few described fractional distillation well: the processes were unfamiliar to many. Thermal cracking and catalytic cracking were both accepted for the name.
findings.rule: Any three of: evaporated; condenses; where the temperature matches the boiling point; continuous.

insight.ruleToRemember: Crude oil is a finite mixture of hydrocarbons. In the column it evaporates, rises and cools, and each fraction condenses where the temperature matches its boiling point; long chains condense low down. Cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter, more useful molecules, some of them alkenes.
insight.aStarSignal: Reading any boiling point against a column to name the fraction, and completing a cracking equation by conserving the atoms.
